claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state.
Phase stability in this alloy is governed by competition between a composition-dependent thermodynamic ordering drive and diffusion-limited kinetics.
Al has a negative mixing enthalpy with late transition metals such as Ni and Co.
The negative Al–Ni or Al–Co mixing enthalpy produces a thermodynamic driving force for local chemical ordering.
Atomic mobility in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is sluggish, particularly for Al and Cr.
The sluggish mobility of Al and Cr makes the phase transformation strongly dependent on cooling rate.
Preferential bonding between Al and late transition metals generates chemical short-range order and ordered clusters.
Ordered secondary phases may nucleate both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Slow cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for the formation and growth of ordered domains.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and nucleation sufficiently to retain the high-temperature BCC phase metastably.
Slow cooling will partially transform the BCC phase into a microstructure containing detectable B2 or L12 ordered precipitates.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain a metastable single-phase BCC structure.
The ordered-phase volume fraction will increase as cooling rate decreases.
The proposed mechanism applies in a regime where diffusion is slow enough to be rate limiting but remains sufficient during slow cooling to permit ordering.
The mechanism may not generalize to alloys with substantially different Al contents.
Cooling rates above 100 °C/s and below 10 °C/s are proposed as rapid-quench and slow-cooling comparison regimes, respectively.
A lack of a significant cooling-rate-dependent difference in ordered-phase fraction or transformation behavior would falsify the proposed kinetic–thermodynamic explanation.
Failure to observe the predicted ordered phases even under slow cooling would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions include cooling into temperatures where ordering is thermodynamically favorable, whereas the boundary describes the applicable range as being above the onset of ordering. Read literally as a temperature bound, the latter excludes the lower-temperature regime in which the predicted ordering is supposed to occur.
